notes.text: Palm leaves shaped this script: a straight stroke would split the leaf, so Odia letters curve instead.
Namaskar works everywhere, but in western Odisha people say juhar, a greeting that doubles as a bow of respect.
Being polite changes the verb, not just the pronoun: tume karucha for a friend, apana karuchanti for an elder.
Your father's elder brother is bada bapa, big father; his younger brother is sana bapa. Age is built in.
Pakhala, rice left overnight in water, has its own day every March. Odias abroad post photos of it.
Old markets count by gonda, a set of four, and pana, twenty gonda. Fish is still sold that way.
Haladia, yellow, is simply turmeric coloured. Kamala, orange, is just the fruit. Odia names colours after what grows.
Leaving a house, never say jauchi, I am going. Say asuchi, I am coming, so the return is promised.
Kali means yesterday and tomorrow both. Gata kali points back, asanta kali points forward, and context does the rest.
The first sale of the day is bohni. Shopkeepers often shave the price for it, so bargain early.
Nobody says I have a headache. The head does the acting: mo mundha bethuchi, my head is paining.
People say ama ghara, our house, even when it is only theirs. Claiming a home alone sounds a bit cold.
Kama is any work; chakiri, borrowed from Persian, means a salaried job. Relatives usually mean chakiri when they ask.
Abhimana is the sulk you feel only toward someone you love. English needs a sentence; Odia needs one word.
During Raja, three days in June, the earth is said to be menstruating. No ploughing, and everyone swings.
